  • If education is the goal, fund a 529 first. It's the best tax deal for college and trade-school costs, and many states sweeten it further.
  • If your child qualifies for the pilot deposit, claim the Trump Account regardless. The $1,000 seed costs you nothing and compounds for nearly two decades.
  • If you want flexibility — savings that could become a down payment, seed capital, or a retirement head start — additional Trump Account contributions fit that role.

Two things to keep straight. First, Trump Account contributions are not tax-deductible, so don't fund one expecting a tax break this year. Second, the $1,000 pilot is only for the 2025–2028 birth window — children born earlier can still open an account, they just don't get the seed money.

The biggest mistake would be letting the shiny new option distract from the boring basics: the account that actually gets funded wins. An automatic monthly contribution to either account beats a perfect strategy you never start.

Educational content only — this is general guidance, not financial advice. Tax rules change; check current IRS guidance before opening or funding any account.

articles.title: The Winter Heating Bill Playbook: 12 Moves to Cut Your Cold-Weather Energy Costs
articles.excerpt: Realtor.com is warning about a painful heating season, and utilities are saying the same thing. You can't control fuel prices, but you can control how much of it your home burns — and how much assistance you claim.
articles.html:
1. Turn the thermostat down when you're asleep or away

The single highest-leverage move is free. The Department of Energy estimates that setting the thermostat back 7–10 degrees for about eight hours a day can cut your heating costs by up to 10% over the year. Set it before bed and when the house is empty; a programmable or smart thermostat does this automatically so you don't have to remember.

2. Get on budget billing before the first big bill

Most utilities let you spread winter costs across the year in equal monthly payments. You still pay for everything you use, but January and February stop being $300 gut-punches. Call your utility and ask — enrollment often closes once heating season starts, so do it this month.

3. Stop drafts at their source

A dollar of heat leaking under the front door costs the same as a dollar of heat from the furnace. Run your hand around exterior doors, windows, and baseboards on a windy day. Weatherstripping and door sweeps are cheap, and a tube of caulk handles gaps around window frames and where pipes enter the house.

4. Seal the chimney when it's not in use

An open fireplace damper is an open window to the roof. Close it every time the fire is fully out, and consider an inflatable chimney plug if you rarely use the fireplace — just remember it's in there before lighting the next fire.

5. Keep the furnace or boiler serviced

A heating system with a dirty filter or neglected burners runs longer to produce the same heat. Change the filter monthly during heating season and get the system serviced once a year before the cold arrives. If it makes new noises, short-cycles, or heats unevenly, that's a repair to make now — mid-January emergency calls are never cheaper.

6. Bleed the radiators (if you have them)

Radiators with air trapped inside heat unevenly — hot at the bottom, cold at the top. A radiator key costs almost nothing; open the bleed valve until water runs steadily, then close it. Do this at the start of the season and your system runs shorter cycles.

7. Let the sun in, keep curtains closed at night

South-facing windows are free daytime heat. Open the curtains in the morning, then close everything at dusk — windows are the thinnest part of your insulation. Heavy or thermal curtains help more than thin ones.

8. Check your attic insulation

Heat rises, and an under-insulated attic is the most common place it escapes. If you can see the ceiling joists poking through the insulation, you probably don't have enough. Adding insulation is one of the few upgrades that pays for itself quickly — but get multiple quotes if you're hiring it out.

9. Ask your utility about a free home energy audit

Many utilities offer free or discounted home energy assessments, sometimes with free weatherization supplies thrown in. Search your utility's name plus "energy audit" or call and ask. Some states also run weatherization assistance programs that pay for insulation, sealing, and furnace repairs for qualifying households.

10. Look into LIHEAP if money is tight

The federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) helps qualifying households pay heating and cooling bills. Funding is distributed through state and local agencies, and applications typically open in the fall — meaning now. Search "LIHEAP" plus your state to find your local office and the income limits. The program can also cover crisis assistance for households at risk of shutoff.

11. Lower the water heater temperature

Your water heater is often the second-biggest energy user in the house. Most are set at 140 degrees; 120 is hot enough for showers, laundry, and dishwashers in most homes, and it lowers the standby cost all winter. Insulate the tank and the first few feet of hot-water pipe for extra savings.

12. Compare delivery and supply rates if your state allows choice

In deregulated states you can sometimes choose your electricity or natural-gas supplier separately from the utility that delivers it. The utility's own default rate is the safe benchmark — compare third-party offers against it, watch for teaser rates that reset higher, and never let a door-to-door sales rep rush you into a contract.

The bottom line

You don't need a renovation to take the edge off heating season. Drop the thermostat on a schedule, seal the leaks you can feel with your hand, get on budget billing, and check whether LIHEAP or a free audit is available in your area. Do the free things this week and the rest before the first real cold snap.

articles.title: The October-to-December Money Checklist: 9 Moves to Make Before the Year Ends
articles.excerpt: Tax rules run on a calendar, not your convenience. With about ten weeks left in the year, these are the moves worth checking off now — while there's still time to act.
articles.html:
1. Check your 401(k) contributions

If you contribute to a 401(k) at work, the IRS lets you put in money until December 31 — no extensions. Pull up your year-to-date contributions and compare them against the annual limit and, if you're 50 or older, the catch-up allowance. If you're on track to fall short of what you planned, you can usually bump up your per-paycheck percentage for the remaining pay periods. Most payroll systems take one to two cycles to process a change, so mid-October is genuinely the last comfortable moment to adjust.

2. Spend down your FSA — or check what your plan lets you do

Flexible Spending Account money is mostly "use it or lose it." Some employers offer a grace period into early next year, and others allow a small rollover amount — but many plans still forfeit unspent balances. Log into your FSA portal, see your remaining balance, and plan for real expenses: prescription refills, a dentist visit, new glasses, sunscreen, first-aid supplies. Don't invent spending just to zero it out; but don't donate your own money back to your employer by forgetting.

3. Consider tax-loss harvesting in taxable accounts

If you own investments outside retirement accounts that are currently underwater, selling some of them can generate a capital loss that offsets gains elsewhere (or up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year, with the rest carrying forward). Two rules matter: the wash-sale rule means you can't buy back the same or a "substantially identical" security within 30 days before or after the sale — including in your IRA — and you should never sell just for the tax break if the investment still belongs in your plan. This is a rebalancing move with a tax bonus, not the other way around.

4. Think about a Roth conversion — carefully

If your income is temporarily low this year (job change, sabbatical, a gap between gigs), converting some of a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA may cost less in taxes than it would in a normal year. But conversions are irreversible and the converted amount counts as taxable income now, so run the numbers on what the extra income does to your tax bracket — and to things tied to your income, like ACA premium credits or Medicare premiums down the road. When in doubt, convert a modest slice rather than going all-in.

5. Give to charity the tax-smart way

If you itemize deductions, contributions to qualified charities reduce your taxable income — but only if they're made by December 31, and only to eligible organizations (check the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search). Two smarter-than-cash options: donating appreciated stock lets you deduct the fair market value while never paying capital gains tax on the appreciation, and if you're 70½ or older, a qualified charitable distribution directly from your IRA counts toward required minimum distributions without being taxed as income.

6. Top off your HSA if you can

Health Savings Account contributions reduce your taxable income dollar for dollar, and unlike the FSA there's no use-it-or-lose-it rule — the balance is yours forever and grows tax-free. If you're in an HSA-eligible high-deductible plan and haven't hit the annual limit, extra contributions before year-end lower this year's tax bill and build a medical fund for later. Just watch the limit: exceeding it triggers penalties.

7. Confirm your required minimum distributions

If you're 73 or older (the current RMD starting age) and hold traditional IRAs or 401(k)s, you generally must take your required minimum distribution by December 31. Miss it and the penalty is steep. Most custodians will calculate the amount for you and can automate the withdrawal — but it's your responsibility, not theirs, to make sure it happens.

8. Review withholding before a surprise, not after

Did you get a raise, a bonus, freelance income, or a new spouse this year? Each of those can quietly change what you owe. The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator is free and takes a few minutes. Adjusting your W-4 now gives you a couple of paychecks to absorb the change; discovering a shortfall in April costs you interest and possibly penalties. Small estimated-tax payments in the fourth quarter can also cover side-income gaps.

9. Harvest your gains strategically, too

Tax-loss harvesting gets the headlines, but if you're in the 0% long-term capital gains bracket (which covers a surprising amount of middle-income retirees and part-year workers), selling winners at no tax cost and rebuying can "step up" your cost basis for free. Again: only with money that already belongs in your plan, and only after confirming your actual bracket with real numbers.

The honest bottom line

None of these moves makes anyone rich. What they do is stop the calendar from quietly costing you money — forfeited FSA balances, missed contribution room, penalties, or a tax bill you could have softened. Block an hour this weekend, work the list top to bottom, and start January with nothing hanging over you. That's what a good year-end looks like.
